nameStory: The 'scented hosta' gets its name from being the only fragrant member of the hosta family - most hostas have no scent at all! It's also called 'August lily' because its white, trumpet-shaped flowers bloom in late summer when most other hostas are finished flowering. The sweet fragrance is so strong it can perfume an entire garden corner on warm evenings.
description: Scented hosta is a medium-sized perennial plant with broad, heart-shaped leaves that form attractive clumps in shady spots. The plant grows about 2-3 feet tall and wide, with glossy green leaves that have prominent veins running from base to tip. In late summer, tall flower spikes emerge with pure white, trumpet-shaped blooms that release an intense, sweet fragrance. Originally from China, this garden favorite occasionally escapes cultivation but is quite rare in the wild in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white, trumpet-shaped flowers about 4 inches long that bloom in late summer, releasing an incredibly sweet, almost intoxicating fragrance especially in evening - no other hosta smells this amazing

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, heart-shaped leaves with a glossy, almost waxy feel and prominent parallel veins that curve from the base to the pointed tip, bright to medium green color

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat, symmetrical clumps 2-3 feet tall and wide, with leaves emerging directly from the ground in a fountain-like arrangement

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flower spikes rise well above the foliage on sturdy stems, with multiple blooms opening from bottom to top over several weeks in August and September

habitat: In New England, scented hosta is almost exclusively found as a garden escape near old house sites, abandoned gardens, or where garden waste has been dumped. It prefers partial shade and rich, moist soil, typically growing along woodland edges or in naturalized areas where it can spread slowly by underground stems.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as pointed shoots (called 'pips') pushing through the soil, unfurling into the characteristic heart shape as they grow larger through late spring.
seasonality.summer: Foliage is at its peak lushness in early to mid-summer, with flower buds beginning to form on tall spikes in July, leading to the spectacular fragrant bloom period in August.
seasonality.fall: After flowering, seed pods may form, and leaves begin to yellow and die back with first frost, leaving only underground roots and stems.
seasonality.winter: Plant is completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, but the crown (where stems meet roots) can be found just below soil surface.

funFact: Scented hosta flowers are so intensely fragrant that in China, people traditionally placed the blooms indoors to perfume entire rooms, and the sweet scent is said to be strongest on humid evenings when it can be detected from 20 feet away!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other large hostas, but the incredible fragrance of the white flowers is a dead giveaway - if you can smell sweet perfume from a hosta bloom, you've found the scented species! Other hostas may have white or pale flowers, but they're essentially scentless.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'plantain lily' along with other hostas, these plants are not related to either plantain weeds or true lilies - they're actually in the agave family. The name comes from the ribbed leaves that somewhat resemble the common plantain weed that grows in lawns.
compareHints: Scented hosta is the only fragrant species among all hostas - this alone sets it apart from blue plantain-lily, Siebold's plantain lily, and other relatives. It also blooms much later than most hostas (August rather than June-July) and has the largest, most trumpet-like flowers. While other hostas may have white flowers, theirs are smaller, bell-shaped, and completely without scent.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Blue Plantain-lily stands out from other hostas by its blue-green leaf color and substantial, waxy texture.
Among New England hostas, small-leaved plantain lily is the most compact species with proportionally smaller leaves than blue plantain lily or Siebold's plantain lily.
Among hostas, this species is unmistakable due to its narrow leaves - all other common New England hostas have much broader, heart-shaped or oval foliage.
Siebold's Plantain Lily stands out from other hostas by its exceptional size and that distinctive blue-gray, waxy leaf texture.
